question: LVP vs porcelain tile: which is better for a Florida house?
title: LVP vs Porcelain Tile for a Florida House
h1: LVP or Porcelain Tile: Which Is Better for a Florida House?
description: A two-person crew lays about 1,000 sq ft of click LVP in 1-2 days; porcelain takes longer. Compare cost and durability for Sarasota homes.
capsule: For most Sarasota-area homes, LVP installs faster and costs less than porcelain tile — a two-person crew can lay about 1,000 square feet of click LVP in 1-2 days on a flat, prepped slab, while tile takes longer because of cure times. Our verdict: choose LVP for speed and warmth underfoot, porcelain for wet areas and long-term durability.

sections.h2: Which Is Better for a Florida House, LVP or Porcelain Tile?
sections.html:
Both materials are effectively waterproof, so the decision usually comes down to timeline, budget and how the room gets used. A two-person crew can install roughly 1,000 sq ft of click-together LVP in one to two days on a flat, prepped slab. Porcelain tile takes several times longer, because thinset and grout need cure time between steps, and that adds up fast if you're re-flooring a whole house instead of one bathroom.

Cost tracks the same pattern. This Old House puts national installed LVP costs at roughly $5-$20 per sq ft depending on product grade, while porcelain typically runs higher once labor for cutting and setting is factored in. For a house you're not planning to leave for months, that install-time gap is often the deciding factor as much as price. We saw this play out on a 1,800 sq ft single-story home off Bee Ridge Road last season: the owners had budgeted for tile throughout, then switched the bedrooms and hallway to LVP once they realized the whole project would run nearly two weeks longer with tile in every room instead of four days.

The install-pace gap widens even more on a two-story job, since tile setters generally can't stack loaded thinset trowels and grout buckets on stairs the way an LVP crew can carry pre-cut planks up in bundles.

Porcelain wins on raw durability and water performance. To legally carry the name, a tile has to absorb 0.5% water or less under ANSI A137.1, tested to ASTM C373 — that's a lab standard, not a sales pitch, and it's why a shower pan or a Siesta Key lanai transition holds up to standing water better under tile than under almost anything else. Porcelain also doesn't scratch the way vinyl can under grit or furniture legs, which matters in an entryway that sees beach traffic all summer.

The tradeoff is comfort and noise. Tile is cold underfoot in January and loud with hard-sole shoes or a dog's nails, and grout lines need periodic sealing, typically every one to two years, to stay stain-resistant. Large-format porcelain reduces the grout-line count and softens that noise issue somewhat, though it also demands a flatter slab to install correctly.

LVP wins on speed, upfront cost and comfort. It installs faster, flexes slightly so it's easier on your feet and back over a long day, and a scratched or damaged plank can be replaced individually instead of chiseling out thinset. The one real weak spot is sun: COREtec's own installation guide warns against prolonged direct sunlight on vinyl planks and recommends drapes or blinds during peak hours, because heat buildup can cause discoloration and thermal expansion at a west-facing sliding door.

Plenty of our clients don't pick one exclusively. A common approach in this market is porcelain in the kitchen, entry and bathrooms, with LVP running through bedrooms and living areas, which keeps the highest-wear, wettest rooms on the more durable material without paying tile pricing across the whole square footage. Not sure which split fits your specific rooms and budget? faqs.q: Is LVP or tile better for a kitchen?
faqs.a: Either works, but porcelain handles grease, heat near the stove and heavy dropped-pan impacts slightly better. Many Sarasota kitchens use wood-look porcelain for that reason and pair it with LVP in adjoining living areas.

faqs.q: Does LVP scratch easier than tile?
faqs.a: Yes, especially thinner 12-mil products. A 20-mil wear layer closes most of that gap; see our guide on choosing a 12-mil or 20-mil wear layer.

faqs.q: Which one is easier to repair?
faqs.a: LVP, in most cases. A damaged plank can be swapped without disturbing the rest of the floor, while a cracked tile usually means chiseling out thinset around it.
